As you [probably know], coffee is the [second largest commodity] by traded value in the world, after oil. You probably also know that it's grown in Brazil, but you may not realize that it's not native to that country. It originated in East Africa. So if it came from there, how did it cross the Pacific? Well, the Dutch took coffee to a number of different places around the world, including, including South America, where it thrived. Nowadays, all the coffee cultivated in Brazil comes from that one seedling, which was of a variety called robusto. Now, because it all comes from the one plant, genetically, robusto isn't particularly varied, which unfortunately means its resistance to disease is, well, rather on the low side. And, well, this is exactly what has happened recently. A pathogen called coffee rust is ravaging coffee crops across South America. So what it looks like is that the price of coffee is, well, going to skyrocket on the wholesale markets unless production is increased dramatically in a short space of time in other countries, such as, you know, Vietnam, which seems rather unlikely. So, in short, there's a good chance that your morning coffee is going to become, well, quite pricey, and pretty soon at that.

I think there are a [lot of confusing messages] about health and [food out there] that don't really help the cause. Look at the most recent debate, fat versus sugar. Two things that we know scientifically are of concern. And I think a big problem is that in the field of nutrition science, we look at individual nutrients like fat,

carbohydrate, protein, etc. To figure out the metabolic consequences of food. And so when we're putting out public guidance about what we should be eating, we talk in terms of nutrients instead of converting those nutrients into foods like fish, fruit, cookies and so on. But I think talking about foods rather than nutrients is an important step we need to take. At the same time, we don't have to say to people, you can eat this or you can't eat that, but we should help give people a

wider view of the relative proportions of various food groups and dietary patterns. On the whole.

Artificial intelligence is transforming the healthcare industry by providing doctors with advanced tools for diagnostic accuracy and patient care. By analyzing massive datasets, these machine learning algorithms can identify subtle patterns in medical imaging that the human eye might overlook. This technological integration ensures more precise treatment plans and significantly reduces the margin of error in clinical environments for better health outcomes.
